metadata.title: Le Chatelier: add A, Q falls below K, the system shifts forward
metadata.subject: Chemistry
metadata.objective: Show how a concentration change shifts an equilibrium and why the shift counteracts the disturbance.
misconceptions: Adding reactant always increases product yield without limit
The equilibrium position is the same thing as the rate
metadata.expectedUnderstanding: For A going to B, Q = [B] / [A]. Adding A raises the denominator, so Q drops below K. Q below K means the forward reaction outpaces the reverse one, so A is consumed and B is produced until Q returns to K. The equilibrium position has moved, K has not: the tick stays fixed because K depends only on temperature. Because A is left at a higher level each time, equal additions raise [B] by smaller and smaller amounts, and the conversion never goes to completion.

primitives.text: Le Chatelier: add A, Q falls below K, the system shifts forward
Q = [B] / [A], where the system sits now

checkpoints.prompt: At the start Q sits exactly on the tick marked K and both arrows are equally strong. Have the two reactions stopped?
A was just added, so Q is now below K. Which direction must the system move to bring Q back to K?
Continue and watch the marker and the two arrows as the reaction proceeds. Which one changes: the position of Q, or the tick for K?
The second addition produced a smaller rise in [B] than the first. Why does the yield not grow without limit?

narration.text: At equilibrium both arrows are equally strong: both reactions are still running, at the same rate, so nothing changes on net.
Q is the ratio [B] over [A], and it currently sits exactly on the tick marked K.
Now more A is added. The A bar jumps up, the ratio falls, and the marker slides left: Q is below K.
With Q below K the forward reaction outpaces the reverse one, so the system shifts to the right: A is consumed and B is produced.
As B builds and A falls, Q climbs back toward K. The position shifted; the K tick did not move, because K depends only on temperature.
A second equal addition of A gives a smaller rise in B, because some A is left over each time, so Q returns to K after a smaller change in B.
The system stops shifting only when Q equals K again. Adding reactant never converts everything: the yield rises in ever smaller steps.

fallback.text: Static side-by-side figure. Left: two bars for [A] and [B] on a common baseline; right: a horizontal Q scale from 0 to 2 with a fixed vertical tick at Q = 1 labelled K, and a filled dot marking Q = [B] / [A]. Show three columns. Start: [A] = 1, [B] = 1, Q = 1 exactly on K, both direction arrows the same weight. After adding A: [A] = 3, [B] = 1, Q = 0.33, dot left of K, forward arrow dominant. After the shift: [A] = 2, [B] = 2, Q = 1 back on K. A second row repeats the cycle from [A] = 2, [B] = 2: add A to 3, then settle at [A] = 2.5, [B] = 2.5, so the same addition bought only 0.5 of B instead of 1.0. A caption reads: the shift opposes the disturbance, K never moves at fixed temperature, and conversion is never complete.

accessibility.alt: Left: two vertical bars labelled A reactant (red) and B product (blue) on a baseline. Right: a horizontal scale for the reaction quotient Q with a fixed vertical tick marked K, and a red dot that slides along it. Arrows for the forward and reverse reactions sit above the scale, and their weight changes with the dot: when the dot is left of K the forward arrow is strongest, when it is right of K the reverse arrow is strongest, and when it is on K both are equal. When A is added the A bar rises and the dot jumps left, then the dot drifts back to K as the A bar falls and the B bar rises.
accessibility.reducedMotion: Show four static frames of the same two panels: equilibrium ([A] = 1, [B] = 1, Q on K), the instant after adding A ([A] = 3, Q = 0.33 left of K, forward arrow dominant), the second equilibrium ([A] = 2, [B] = 2, Q back on K), and the smaller increment from adding A again ([A] = 2.5, [B] = 2.5).
